newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Europe convergence plays dealt a blow. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Europe convergence plays dealt a blow. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]

text.p: European bond convergence trades will grind to a halt unless investors are satisfied that fiscal prudence will continue after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Wednesday.
French plans to use a payment from France Telecom to reduce its budget deficit have met with criticism from a Bundesbank council member and opposition from some EU states.
Analysts said investors now need more details on plans for a "stability pact" -- designed to ensure fiscal responsibility after EMU -- if European yields are to converge further.

"The stability pact has got to go through in a solid form to satisfy the markets," said Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Markets in London. "The flow of European money into convergence trades has slowed."
The European Commission earlier this month put forward a draft proposal for a stability pact which suggested countries running a budget deficit higher than 3.0 percent of GDP would face sanctions.
But the proposal did not detail the size of sanctions or fines and failed to define the "exceptional and temporary" circumstance which would allow a country to exeed specified budget deficit limits.
"It's full of loopholes," said Andy Bevan, senior international bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London. "There are no definitions and too many catch-alls."
He said the eruption of bickering in the last few days over EMU had been fed by the woolly wording of the pact, and would not be calmed until the Commission had specified proposals.
"They've got to do that before the heads of government meeting in December," said Bevan. "It's a general worry now."
European Union heads of state will meet in Dublin on December 13-14.
Although Bevan said debt markets still remain confident that EMU will go ahead at the start date of January 1999, investors are unwilling to put on more convergence trades at the moment.

The French government is confident the Commission will approve its decision to use a one-off payment from France Telecom to cut its budget. But Bundesbank central council member Raimut Jochimsen on Tuesday attacked the move.
He said the German public would not accept a single currency based on a "fudging" of the Maastricht treaty criteria.
Then on Wednesday, a Commission source said German, Britain and Dutch officials sitting on a European statistics committee had argued against allowing France to use the transfer.

Juckes said bond markets had already done so well this year, that investors were starting to question their next move. "Yield levels, such as Bunds at 6.0 percent, have got to places where the market is not sure how much further it can go," he said. Bevan advised investors involved into convergence trades to take some profits and protect their remaining exposure.

He advised buying six-month call options on 10-year bond spreads and selling a put on the spread out of the money (corrects from (".. spread deep in the money..")) to finance it. Another trade he suggested was buying BTP puts and selling Bund puts to pay for it.
"Lots of people are doing these trades since they became more rattled,"said Bevan.
Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns International in London, said convergence trades should have a further leg, although they were now more risky.
"But irrespective of the European debate, the fundamentals of the high yielders are likely to improve to the year end, and that will provide support," he said.

Shute said the bond market was still vulnerable to EMU related worries, such as those which were raised over France. "If it is ruled that this (French payment) is not legitimate, then that will create an adverse market reation," Shute said.
